A 48-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for acid reflux over the last 3 months. He has
been trying over-the-counter calcium carbonate tablets almost daily, which have provided minimal
relief. He denies any difficulty or pain with swallowing, weight loss, bloody vomitus, dark-colored stools,
or night sweats. He has a medical history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia and has smoked 1 pack
of cigarettes daily for the last 20 years. He takes lisinopril and atorvastatin daily. His temperature is

99.1°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 116/79 mmHg, pulse is 61/min, and respirations are 20/min. His
body mass index is 33 kg/m^2. Physical examination discloses no abnormalities. The patient is
scheduled for an endoscopy, which demonstrates salmon-colored esophageal mucosa at the
gastroesophageal junction. A biopsy of this mucosa demonstrates no dysplasia or evidence of
Helicobacter pylori infection. He is started on proton pump inhibitor therapy, as well as nicotine and
dietary counseling. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? Answer
Choices: (A) Screening for esophageal adenocarcinoma annually (B) Proton pump inhibitor therapy
only (C) Referral for esophageal manometry (D) Barium swallow study (E) Repeat endoscopy in 3-5
years (F) Lifestyle modification without further endoscopic follow-up (G) Testing for Helicobacter pylori
eradication (H) Antireflux surgery (I) Repeat endoscopy in 6-12 months (J) Repeat endoscopy in 1-2
years
 A. Proton pump inhibitor therapy only
B. Repeat endoscopy in 6-12 months
C. Testing for Helicobacter pylori eradication
D. Referral for esophageal manometry
E. Repeat endoscopy in 1-2 years
F. Barium swallow study
G. Screening for esophageal adenocarcinoma annually
H. Antireflux surgery
I. Repeat endoscopy in 3-5 years
J. Lifestyle modification without further endoscopic follow-up
